title: Mastering Chess Flexibility | King's Indian and Philidor | GM Naroditsky's DYI Speedrun

moves.spoken: White opens d4 and we answer with a knight to f6, heading for a King's Indian setup.
White grabs the center with c4.
We fianchetto with g6 — another King's Indian.
And White plays the modest e3.
A couple of games ago we faced a similar offbeat setup with a knight to c3 and a bishop to e3.

Until we climb past 1500-1600 we won't often see the main King's Indian lines, which is exactly why you lay the groundwork of understanding the ideas — so you can react when your opponent throws something unexpected.
We complete the fianchetto with a bishop to g7.
White adds b3 — a double-fianchetto setup.
It's impossible to memorize all of White's possible setups; there are a million of them.
The important thing is to understand which setup you're going for and how to react to your opponent's.
White is just playing moves — e3, b3 — and that doesn't really change our reaction.
So the first step is to play all the standard King's Indian moves. We castle.

White plays a bishop to b2, and now the big decision I discussed last game: the traditional King's Indian is to prepare d6 and e5, but the modern understanding is that against some setups it's more efficient to play Benoni-style with c5, or even Grünfeld-style with d5. Stay flexible about which pawn break you choose. Against this setup a case can be made for either c5 or preparing e5.

The c5 break tempts, since it would create a bishop standoff with White's king still in the center — but I also want to show the classic King's Indian way, so let's play d6 and carry out the e5 break even with White's bishop already on b2.
White plays a knight to c3, trying to discourage e5 — but the great thing about the King's Indian is you can usually force that break anyway. Still, this changes my thinking a little.

The problem with e5 now is that it allows a queen trade, and I want more than an endgame. So because White played the knight to c3, I like c5 a lot more — after White's standard d5, we have a tactic: a knight to e4, exposing the bishop on b2 and grabbing the bishop pair.
White develops a knight to f3. We're going to pressure White's center, but carefully.

A knight to c6 right now would let White push d5 with tempo, so we reserve it and start with a queen to a5 — a very challenging move, already setting up the knight-to-e4 idea while we play on the queenside.
White plays a bishop to d3, which stops the knight to e4 — but since the bishop didn't go to e2, we now have a bishop-to-g4 idea for the right moment.
And the right moment isn't yet — the whole point of the queen to a5 was to enable a knight to c6, because now we have a tactic against d5.
White pushes d5, and our pieces come together — we're piling serious pressure on d4. A knight to e4 is the thematic idea, but there's a better execution.

Since we're moving the knight anyway, we grab the pawn with a knight capture on d5 — just winning a pawn. It's easy to calculate: a recapture on d5, and then a bishop to c3 with check trades the bishops and leaves White in shambles.
White recaptures on d5.
The bishop takes on c3 with check — and it's very important that it's a check.
White's position collapses. He can't play a queen to d2, a common reflexive blunder here, because it drops the rook on a1 — a bit of whole-board awareness.
White bites the bullet with the king to e2, but it brings little relief. A common mistake is to win a pawn and rest on your laurels — dropping back or trading knights — but we have a better way.

Don't forget our knight is hanging, but we don't want to stop at one pawn while White's position is collapsing. The instinctive move is a knight to b4 — it hits the pawn, pressures the bishop, and sits very stably.
White is lost. After a rook to c1, we have a really pretty move.
You might expect a knight capture on d5, but I prefer a capture on a2 — it also hits the rook, and if White takes our queen we recapture with a fork.
White takes and walks right into it, and we win — up a ton of material.
The rest is easy: we have a big queenside majority and the extra exchange.
The next step is to open files for our rooks.

A bishop to g4 trading minor pieces is fine, but to win efficiently I want to open a rook's file. Playing a5 immediately creates a weak square on b5 for White's bishop — pedantic here, but let's start with a bishop to d7 to make the a5-a4 push smoother.
Would my opponent really play a bishop to b5 at this level? Probably not.
But the point of the speedrun is to build good habits early.
Now we play a5 — f5 is worse, because pushing to f4 lets White keep things locked up.
White plays a bishop to c2.
Obviously we push b5.
And a4, creating a passed pawn and opening the b-file.
We'll occupy the b-file with our other rook.
White plays a knight to d2.
If White aims for c4, that's no problem — a bishop to b5 pins and pressures the knight.
It doesn't win the knight, but it trades it off, letting our pawn inch forward.
Just trading — I'm playing quickly here.
Everything is simple now — we want to push the pawn toward a2.
A rook to b4, forcing the bishop back.
And a rook to b2, tying the bishop down; if it moves again, a2.
The bishop moves, we push to a2, and it's easy.
People are taught to trade pieces, so they'd give up the a-pawn — but that takes longer to convert, and there's no reason to give it up.
The easier win is to chase the bishop with the other rook, a rook to a4, and push the c-pawn.
This is dull for advanced players, but c3, c2...
The last step is just to get this rook to b1.
A rook to b4.
We don't care what our opponent is doing.
And the pawn promotes.
We recapture on g6.
And our opponent resigns — a simple game. The big blunder came on move nineteen, but it happened because we chose the right pawn break.
Our opponent played e3 — not a bad move in itself...
...if White follows up normally with the main line, a knight to c3 and e4.
That's the entry point to a million King's Indian variations.

With e3 and b3 the engine still reads roughly equal, so don't think of it as terrible. We played d6 and White played a knight to c3 — I expected a knight to f3. Here's an important idea: you can play e5 here, and it looks like a flat-out blunder, but King's Indian players know it. White can hop the knight away, but a knight to d7 is more common, and the e5-push is toast — you attack it three times, White can't defend it, and can't move it because his bishop falls. This idea shows up most against a Zukertort or double-fianchetto b3 setup, where playing a King's Indian in response is completely fine.
